extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in 19th-century American newspaper practice
extracted.subtask_description: Historical overview of newspaper production, content, business practices, technology, and professional norms in U.S. journalism during the Civil War and Reconstruction (c.1860–1872). Useful for understanding period standards for producing and evaluating newspapers and periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from partisan bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing independence from partisan bonds; editors declaring intention to make journals 'thoroughly independent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers increasingly criticized parties with which they were nominally identified; independence could improve credibility but also led to 'bolts' (e.g., Republican papers and Grant's nomination in 1872). Greeley's late-career declaration—'Henceforth it shall be my endeavor to make this a thoroughly independent journal'—is cited as marking a shift away from party-controlled papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperate, dignified editorial manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The public wants 'publication of news and temperate, dignified, gentlemanly explanation and criticism of current events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors were urged to avoid highly personal attacks and vituperation; examples show frequent violation (e.g., Tribune calling the Times 'lies deliberately...'). The rubric favors restraint and civility in editorial tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from journalistic conventions / format variety
rubrics_metrics.description: More variants from the normal in format, makeup, and content than previously; feature material varied widely among papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some papers (e.g., New York Times) printed little feature material, others (e.g., New York Daily Democrat) were valued chiefly for humorous or feature writing. Weekly papers often devoted much of their space to essays, stories, humorous paragraphs, and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and prominence of newspaper poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper poetry had considerable importance (examples: Stedman's 'How Old Brown Took Harper’s Ferry'; Bryant's 'Death of Lincoln').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems were printed in dailies and weeklies and could be major content items, especially during wartime; placement and selection of poetry were seen as part of a paper's literary character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wit, humor, and humorous sketches/columnists
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorists and comic sketches were widespread and influential (e.g., Mark Twain's 'Jumping Frog'; Artemus Ward; Nasby sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humorists' pen-names and sketches were widely reprinted; satire and exaggeration were used as political critique (e.g., making the Copperhead ridiculous). Papers could build national reputation on such material and its reprintability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly papers' greater miscellany
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly papers generally printed a larger proportion of miscellany than dailies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four-page weeklies sometimes devoted large portions of page one to selected essays, stories, and miscellaneous items; they served small communities with a mix of local news, political comment, and advertorial/legal notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine editorial positioning (illustrated vs. literary focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different magazines occupied distinct niches: illustrated general magazines (Harper's, Scribner's) versus higher literary journals without pictures (Atlantic Monthly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers chose format and content to position magazines: illustrated woodcuts and crowded fiction for general appeal; no pictures but high literary standard for prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion and specialization of periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodicals multiplied and specialized (religious, medical, legal, agricultural, educational, industrial, and trade journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth meant many niche publications (stamp collectors, brewers, spiritualists, dentists, railways, insurance, fraternal organizations, etc.), indicating an editorial/market rubric favoring target-audience specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and frontier coverage (western expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers proliferated in midwestern and far western states to serve new towns and territories (e.g., Idaho, Montana, Wyoming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers were founded in mining camps, forts, and newly settled towns to provide local news; logistical factors (distance to nearest paper) influenced existence and format of pioneer papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country weekly format and content expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Country weeklies: four-page papers, six to nine columns per page, circulations usually less than 1,000; content included local news, advertising, miscellany, political comment, legal and patent-medicine notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly every village (~1,000 inhabitants) had two such papers; editors structured content to local needs and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of syndicated 'patent insides' (readyprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syndicated pages ('patent insides' or 'readyprints') supplied understaffed country weeklies with two pre-printed pages, allowing local papers to fill remaining pages with their own type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Device originated during the war and expanded postwar; space was later sold to advertisers to lower costs. Syndication became an important economic model and precursor to broader content syndication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of Sunday editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment and spread of Sunday editions of regular daily papers and standalone Sunday papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunday editions commonly contained more miscellaneous reading though were often not larger than weekday issues; earlier Sabbatarian objections declined during and after the war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising growth and its newspaper placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising increased markedly after the war; some leading papers reserved front pages for leading stories and moved advertising to inside pages, though front-page advertising persisted in many papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement choices signified editorial priorities—front-page news vs. revenue from display advertising; examples include New York Sun and Herald's differing practices and later reversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising agencies, rates, and business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of advertising agencies (George P. Rowell, N. W. Ayer & Son, Lord & Thomas) and the 'advertising list' model (bulk offers across many papers); varied rates (e.g., 25¢ an agate line common; Herald $1 on top page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents bought low and sold high, charged commissions (25–75%), and guaranteed payment to publishers, professionalizing the ad market. Contract rates, column purchases, and list offers influenced revenue strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers' use of current events and celebrity in copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising writers often utilized current events and public figures to attract attention (e.g., referencing Lincoln's beard to promote an ointment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaborations/traveling gimmicks and testimonial-style ads were common (patent medicines, bearded-lady testimonials), showing a rubric that favored topical hooks and sensational copy to drive readership and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic practices and relaxation of strict agate rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxation of the 'tyranny of agate' with increased white space, cuts, display advertising, and use of double-column ads; headlines on news stories kept to single-column measure with multi-deck heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading papers adopted display type and graphical variation; decks (six to twelve lines) with combinations of roman, boldface, capitals, lowercase, and italics were common. Use of white space could improve effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations and cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustration dominated by war maps and woodcut portraits; political cartoons and regular cartoon features appeared (e.g., Bennett’s New York Evening Telegram's Friday cartoon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weeklies and monthlies (Harper's Weekly, Frank Leslie) used lavish illustration; cartoons accompanied by sketches, poems, or playlets, often satirical of political situations or personages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page sizes, stereotyping, and layout freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline of old 'blanket sheets'; introduction of stereotyping allowed removal of strict column rules and enabled variety in makeup (double-column cuts and ads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotyped plates produced solid curved plates fitting press cylinders, freeing layout from the need for full-length column rules and enabling more diverse page designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of web-perfecting presses
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of the web-perfecting press (e.g., Bullock's press for Philadelphia Inquirer, 1863) printing both sides of the paper from a continuous web and increasing speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Web-perfecting presses allowed automatic feeding from reels, printing both sides in one pass ('perfecting'), increasing production rate and enabling larger circulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsprint prices and adoption of wood pulp
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper prices soared during the war; mechanical wood pulp later reduced newsprint costs and began to replace rag stock (early adoption c.1870s, rag content persisted for years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price examples: good paper rose from 7.5¢/lb to as high as 22–28¢/lb during 1861–63, later declining. Early mixes (e.g., 40% wood pulp, 60% rag) illustrate transitional quality/cost tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and pricing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulations increased during the war; papers adjusted single-copy and subscription prices (some rose from two to three/four cents; penny papers later exploited tenement readership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York Herald claims and rival skepticism; some papers cut price to 1¢ and achieved huge circulations (e.g., New York Daily News). Postwar circulation dips and recoveries influenced business models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional idea: public service and editorial/writing proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism in journalism characterized by emphasis on public service and proficiency in writing and editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By midcentury more men of education entered journalism; leading newspapers were run on the idea of journalism as a profession with educated reporters and writers (Tribune staff largely college graduates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education, training, and early attempts at journalism scholarships
rubrics_metrics.description: Early gestures toward formal education for journalism (e.g., General Robert E. Lee's 1869 offer of scholarships and printing-trade tuition arrangements), though no sustained programs yet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The idea of college education for journalists was nascent and largely unrealized; formal journalism instruction would come much later (e.g., Washington and Lee University not establishing programs until decades later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment conditions and pay levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' and reporters' pay after the war: editors on morning papers $25–$60/week; reporters $15–$30; writers generally ill-paid. Women increasingly entered newspaper work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low pay constrained staffing and contributed to use of syndicated content; note early women reporters and columnists (e.g., Emily Verdery Beecher, Gail Hamilton, Grace Greenwood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Period/era transitions as evaluative markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Year 1872 marked 'the end of an era' with deaths/retirements of major editors and a shift toward independent journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in personnel (Bennett, Greeley) and editorial declarations of independence are cited as signals of changing standards and norms in the newspaper field.
